planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist to wet, calcareous soil in full sun to light shade; an obligate wetland species that spreads by rhizomes and thrives in permanently saturated fens, marshes, and wet meadows.

directions: Rush aster bears slender, grass-like foliage and small daisy flowers with white to pale purple rays surrounding cream to pale yellow disc florets that turn purplish with age, blooming from late summer into fall. Unlike most garden-adapted asters, it is an obligate wetland plant restricted to calcareous fens, marshes, swamps, and wet meadows, where its rhizomatous habit helps stabilize saturated soils. Native from Alaska and northern Canada south to Colorado and West Virginia, it provides late-season nectar for bees and other pollinators in wetland habitats where few other composites are still flowering. Best suited to rain gardens, pond margins, and other consistently wet, sunny sites rather than typical dry garden borders.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained, calcareous soil in full sun; adapted to shallow, rocky glade and barrens soils and does not tolerate rich, moist garden beds well.

directions: Barrens silky aster produces rose-purple ray florets around disc florets that shift from pink to purple as they mature, flowering from September into November, later than many other native asters. It is native to a scattered range of calcareous glades, barrens, and prairies east of the Mississippi River, chiefly in northwestern Georgia and northern and central Alabama, where thin rocky soils exclude more aggressive competitors. Its late, long bloom window makes it a valuable nectar source for bees and migrating butterflies at a point in fall when most other flowers have finished. Best grown in lean, dry, alkaline to neutral soils in a rock garden, glade restoration, or dry prairie planting rather than fertile garden loam.
sources: Alabama Plant Atlas (University of West Alabama)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; spreads by rhizomes and self-seeding in old fields, roadside ditches, and moist meadows.

directions: Small white aster carries numerous small flower heads with white rays and a yellowish-to-pinkish central disc, clustered mostly along one side of widely spreading, smooth purple-tinged stems, blooming in late summer and fall. It is native across a broad swath of eastern North America from Maine south to northern Florida and west to Texas and the Midwest, favoring moist old fields, bottomlands, marsh edges, and roadside ditches. The abundant small flowers attract a wide range of short-tongued native bees, flies, and small butterflies during the fall nectar dearth. Its airy, one-sided flower sprays and tolerance of damp soils suit it to naturalized meadow plantings, rain gardens, and moist woodland-edge restorations.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

common_name: Herbstschnee Aster (Autumn Snow White New England Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; German for autumn snow, this white-flowered New England aster selection is valued for its mildew resistance and sturdy, self-supporting habit.

directions: Herbstschnee is a white-flowered German-bred selection of New England aster, bearing open sprays of yellow-centered daisy flowers with numerous narrow white rays from late summer into late autumn, a striking departure from the purple and pink tones typical of the species. Its clump-forming, upright habit and above-average resistance to powdery mildew make it a reliable choice for the back of a perennial border without the floppiness or foliage decline common in older New England aster cultivars. Like other New England asters, it is an important late-season nectar source for bees, butterflies, and migrating monarchs. Combine with ornamental grasses and late goldenrods for a naturalistic fall display.

common_name: Fellowship Aster (Double Pink New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a tall, upright New York aster selection with large, fully double flowers that benefits from staking or grow-through supports.

directions: Fellowship produces large, fully double, clear pink flowers with bright yellow centers held in generous sprays on upright stems from late summer through fall. Its tall, narrow-leaved habit and abundance of bloom make it a classic choice for the middle to back of a mixed perennial border or cutting garden. As with other New York asters, the late-season flowers draw bees, butterflies, and other pollinators when few other nectar sources remain. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring, and watch for powdery mildew in humid conditions with poor air circulation.

common_name: Royal Ruby Aster (Dwarf Mulberry-Red New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, medium-moisture, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a compact, dwarf New York aster selection well suited to small gardens, borders, and containers.

directions: Royal Ruby is a compact, bushy New York aster selection bearing masses of semi-double, rich mulberry-red flowers with bright golden discs on slender, branched stems from late summer into early fall. Its dwarf, self-supporting habit needs no staking and suits small gardens, front-of-border plantings, and containers where taller New York asters would overwhelm the space. The nectar-rich flowers are an important late-season resource for bees and butterflies as summer bloomers fade. Divide every two to three years in spring to maintain compact form and vigor.
